title: Cursors and Loops — And Why to Avoid Them
interviewQuestion: What is a cursor in SQL Server, and why should you generally avoid them? When is a cursor actually the right tool?

story.setup: A factory needs to apply a 10% raise to every worker's paycheck, and there are two very different ways to do it.
scenes: One manager insists on walking to each worker's desk individually, one at a time, filling out a form, walking back to the payroll office, filing it, then walking to the NEXT desk — that's a cursor: OPEN, FETCH NEXT, process, FETCH NEXT again, in a WHILE @@FETCH_STATUS = 0 loop, each trip a full round-trip with its own overhead.

The other manager just sends one memo to the entire payroll system: 'multiply every salary by 1.10, filtered to department 2' — one set-based UPDATE that touches every relevant row in a single operation.
For 10,000 workers, the door-to-door manager takes literally all day (50-1000x slower — think ~30 seconds versus 0.2 seconds); the memo approach finishes almost instantly.

But there IS a moment the door-to-door approach makes sense: handing each employee their own personalized appraisal envelope requires a truly per-person action (EXEC SendAppraisalEmail per row) — some things genuinely cannot be expressed as one memo, and that's exactly when a cursor (or a WHILE loop for safe batching) is the right, deliberate tool.
story.moral: A cursor turns one set operation into N slow round-trips — reach for set-based SQL first, and reserve cursors/loops for genuinely per-row actions or deliberate batching.

analogy: A cursor is a manager walking door-to-door doing payroll one desk at a time; a set-based UPDATE is one memo that updates every relevant paycheck in a single sweep.
explanation: A cursor lets you iterate row-by-row over a result set with DECLARE CURSOR, OPEN, FETCH NEXT into variables inside a WHILE @@FETCH_STATUS = 0 loop, CLOSE, and DEALLOCATE. The problem is that this turns one logical set operation into N separate round-trips, each incurring its own plan execution, locking, and log-write overhead — typically 50 to 1000 times slower than the equivalent set-based statement (a set-based UPDATE finishing in 0.2 seconds versus roughly 30 seconds for the row-by-row cursor equivalent on the same data). Most cursor-shaped problems have set-based replacements: running totals become SUM() OVER(...), previous-row comparisons become LAG()/LEAD(), numbering becomes ROW_NUMBER(), string concatenation across rows becomes STRING_AGG, and conditional insert-or-update becomes MERGE. Cursors ARE the right tool when you genuinely need a per-row side effect a SET operation can't express — like calling a stored procedure or sending an email per row — or for admin scripts iterating database metadata (e.g., rebuilding every fragmented index). A plain WHILE loop (not a full cursor) is also the standard pattern for safely batching very large DML operations, deleting a fixed chunk at a time with a brief WAITFOR DELAY between batches to release locks.
interviewAnswerShort: Cursors iterate row-by-row (OPEN/FETCH/WHILE @@FETCH_STATUS=0), which turns one set operation into N slow round-trips, typically 50-1000x slower — prefer set-based rewrites (window functions, MERGE, STRING_AGG); cursors are right only for genuine per-row side effects like EXEC per row, or WHILE loops for safe batching of huge DML.
interviewAnswerDetailed: A cursor declares a result set and iterates it one row at a time using OPEN, FETCH NEXT INTO variables, inside a WHILE @@FETCH_STATUS = 0 loop, then CLOSE and DEALLOCATE to release it. The core problem is performance: each FETCH is effectively its own round-trip with plan execution, lock acquisition, and log-write overhead, so what could be one set-based statement becomes N separate operations — commonly 50 to 1000 times slower, for example a set-based UPDATE finishing in about 0.2 seconds where the row-by-row cursor equivalent takes around 30 seconds on the same data. The good news is most problems that look like they need a cursor actually have clean set-based replacements: a running total becomes SUM() OVER (ORDER BY ...), comparing a row to the previous one becomes LAG()/LEAD(), sequential numbering becomes ROW_NUMBER(), building a delimited string from multiple rows becomes STRING_AGG, and conditional insert-or-update logic becomes MERGE. That said, cursors are genuinely the right tool in a few cases: when you need to call a stored procedure per row with a real side effect a SET operation can't express (like sending an individual appraisal email), for admin/maintenance scripts that iterate database metadata (like rebuilding every fragmented index one at a time), or for logic that's truly sequential in a way window functions can't capture. Separately, a plain WHILE loop (no cursor needed) is the standard, deliberate pattern for batching very large DML — deleting a fixed number of rows at a time (like DELETE TOP (5000)) with a brief WAITFOR DELAY between batches to release locks and avoid one enormous, blocking transaction.

codeExample.explanation: The cursor is justified here only because it triggers a genuine per-row side effect (an email); the raise itself is a one-line set-based UPDATE; the WHILE loop shows deliberate batching, not row-by-row iteration.

mistakes: Writing a cursor to do a bulk UPDATE/INSERT/DELETE that could be expressed as a single set-based statement.
Forgetting CLOSE and DEALLOCATE, leaking cursor resources in long-running sessions.
Not using LOCAL FAST_FORWARD when a simple forward-only, read-only cursor is all that's needed, missing an easy optimization.
Confusing a WHILE loop used for deliberate batching with a cursor doing row-by-row business logic — batching a big DML operation is a legitimate, different use case.
Running one giant unbatched DELETE/UPDATE on millions of rows instead of chunking it, causing long blocking and huge transaction log growth.

followUps.question: Why exactly are cursors so much slower?
followUps.answer: Each FETCH is effectively a separate round-trip with its own plan execution, lock acquisition, and transaction log write, so an operation that could be one set-based statement becomes N discrete operations — typically 50 to 1000 times slower for equivalent work.

followUps.question: Give set-based replacements for common cursor patterns.
followUps.answer: Running totals -> SUM() OVER(...); previous-row comparison -> LAG()/LEAD(); numbering -> ROW_NUMBER(); building a string list across rows -> STRING_AGG; conditional insert-or-update -> MERGE.

followUps.question: When IS a cursor the right choice?
followUps.answer: When you need a genuine per-row EXEC of a stored procedure or other side effect that can't be expressed as a set operation, for admin scripts iterating database metadata (like rebuilding every fragmented index one at a time), or for logic that's genuinely sequential in a way window functions can't express.

memoryHack.oneLiner: Cursor = door-to-door payroll, one desk at a time; set-based UPDATE = one memo updates everyone at once.
memoryHack.mnemonic: C.U.R.S.O.R. = Costly Under Repeated Single-row Operations, Reconsider.
memoryHack.memoryPalace: A manager walking every office door individually with a clipboard (cursor) versus posting a single memo on the payroll system's front door that updates everyone at once (set-based UPDATE) — except for the one door where a truly personal appraisal envelope must be hand-delivered (legitimate per-row side effect).

bestPractices: Always try to express the logic as a single set-based statement before reaching for a cursor.
When a cursor is genuinely necessary, use LOCAL FAST_FORWARD for the best performance on forward-only, read-only iteration.
Always CLOSE and DEALLOCATE cursors explicitly.
Use a WHILE loop with a fixed batch size (and a brief WAITFOR DELAY) to safely chunk large DML operations rather than one unbounded statement.
Reserve cursors for genuine per-row side effects (stored procedure calls, emails) or metadata-driven admin scripts, not everyday business logic.
performanceTips: A set-based rewrite of a cursor-based operation commonly yields a 50-1000x speedup on the same data.
Batching large DML with DELETE/UPDATE TOP (N) in a WHILE loop keeps individual transactions short, reducing blocking and log growth compared to one giant statement.
LOCAL FAST_FORWARD cursors are meaningfully faster than default (dynamic, scrollable) cursors when you only need forward, read-only iteration.

quiz.explanation: Each FETCH in a cursor is its own round-trip with plan execution and logging overhead, commonly making cursor-based approaches 50 to 1000 times slower than a single set-based statement.

quiz.question: Which window function replaces a cursor-based 'compare to previous row' pattern?
quiz.explanation: LAG() and LEAD() directly access a preceding or following row's value within an ordered window, replacing manual row-by-row comparison logic.

quiz.question: What is a legitimate use case for a cursor?
options: Applying a percentage raise to all employees in a department
Calling a stored procedure with a genuine per-row side effect, like sending individual emails
Counting the total number of rows in a table
Filtering rows by a date range
quiz.explanation: A per-row action like EXEC SendAppraisalEmail that can't be expressed as a set operation is exactly the case where a cursor is appropriate.

Most cursor-shaped problems have clean set-based replacements: running totals become SUM() OVER(...), previous-row comparisons become LAG()/LEAD(), numbering becomes ROW_NUMBER(), building a delimited string across rows becomes STRING_AGG, and conditional insert-or-update becomes MERGE. title: Foreign Key/Unique Key Syntax and Normalization
interviewQuestion: Explain FOREIGN KEY and UNIQUE constraint syntax, and what are 1NF, 2NF, and 3NF normalization — when would you deliberately denormalize?

story.setup: A city planning office is designing housing regulations for a new district, trying to avoid duplicated, inconsistent paperwork across offices.
scenes: 1NF (First Normal Form) says: every form field must hold one single, atomic answer, not a scribbled comma-separated list — no repeating groups crammed into one box.

2NF says: if a form is identified by a composite key (say, Building + Unit), every other fact on that form must depend on the WHOLE combination, not just part of it — a fact that only depends on Building shouldn't be duplicated on every Unit's form.

3NF says: every fact on the form must depend directly on the form's own ID, not indirectly through some other fact already on that form — if 'City Tax Rate' depends on 'ZipCode' which is itself just a fact on the form, City Tax Rate shouldn't live there redundantly; it belongs on its own ZipCode-keyed form.

The office also enforces that every apartment's paperwork must reference a real, registered landlord (FOREIGN KEY), and later realizes the public reporting dashboard is painfully slow joining five offices' forms together for every report — so, deliberately and with measurement, they start keeping a duplicated summary sheet just for reporting (denormalization for read performance).
story.moral: Normalize the transactional forms to eliminate redundancy and inconsistency; denormalize only deliberately, and only where read performance genuinely demands it.

analogy: Normalization is city paperwork rules that stop the same fact from being scribbled inconsistently on ten different forms; a foreign key is a rule that every apartment's paperwork must name a landlord who's actually registered in the city system.
explanation: FOREIGN KEY constraints enforce referential integrity, ensuring a column's value exists in a referenced parent table's key, optionally with ON DELETE CASCADE / ON UPDATE CASCADE to automatically propagate deletions or key changes to dependent rows. UNIQUE constraints prevent duplicate values while allowing exactly one NULL. Normalization organizes data to reduce redundancy and prevent update anomalies: 1NF requires atomic values with no repeating groups in a single field; 2NF (building on 1NF) eliminates partial dependency, meaning every non-key column must depend on the WHOLE of a composite primary key, not just part of it; 3NF (building on 2NF) eliminates transitive dependency, meaning non-key columns must depend only on the key, not on other non-key columns. Denormalization is the deliberate, measured reintroduction of redundancy — duplicating data to avoid expensive joins in read-heavy reporting scenarios. The senior-level framing: normalize for transactional integrity, denormalize selectively for read performance where measurement justifies it.
interviewAnswerShort: FOREIGN KEY enforces that a value exists in a parent table (optionally cascading); UNIQUE prevents duplicates (one NULL allowed). 1NF = atomic values, 2NF = no partial dependency on a composite key, 3NF = no transitive dependency on non-key columns. Normalize for integrity, denormalize selectively and deliberately for measured read performance.
interviewAnswerDetailed: A FOREIGN KEY constraint ensures a column's value must exist as a key value in a referenced parent table, maintaining referential integrity — you can attach ON DELETE CASCADE and ON UPDATE CASCADE so that deleting or renaming a parent key automatically propagates to dependent child rows, though this needs careful use since cascades can have a wide, sometimes surprising blast radius. A UNIQUE constraint prevents duplicate values across rows while still permitting exactly one NULL, and unlike a primary key, a table can have several UNIQUE constraints. Normalization is the discipline of organizing schema to reduce redundancy and prevent update anomalies, built up in stages: 1NF requires every column to hold a single atomic value with no repeating groups packed into one field; 2NF builds on that by eliminating partial dependency — every non-key column must depend on the entire composite primary key, not just part of it, which matters specifically for tables with multi-column keys; 3NF builds further by eliminating transitive dependency — a non-key column shouldn't depend on another non-key column, only directly on the key itself, so derived or indirectly-related facts get their own table. Denormalization is the deliberate opposite move: intentionally duplicating data to avoid expensive multi-table joins, typically in read-heavy reporting or analytics contexts where join cost has been measured and shown to be a real bottleneck. My senior-level framing for an interviewer is: normalize the transactional schema for data integrity and to avoid update anomalies, and denormalize selectively, deliberately, and only where profiling justifies it — not as a starting design choice.

codeExample.code:
CREATE TABLE Employees (
  EmpId INT PRIMARY KEY,
  Email VARCHAR(100),
  DeptId INT,
  CONSTRAINT UQ_Emp_Email UNIQUE (Email),
  CONSTRAINT FK_Emp_Dept FOREIGN KEY (DeptId) REFERENCES Departments(DeptId)
    ON DELETE CASCADE ON UPDATE CASCADE
);
codeExample.explanation: UQ_Emp_Email enforces no duplicate emails (one NULL allowed); FK_Emp_Dept enforces that DeptId must reference a real department and cascades both deletes and key updates.

mistakes: Applying ON DELETE CASCADE without considering how far the cascade could ripple through related child tables.
Confusing 2NF and 3NF — 2NF is specifically about partial dependency on a COMPOSITE key (irrelevant for single-column keys), while 3NF is about transitive dependency through other non-key columns.
Denormalizing prematurely, before measuring that joins are actually a real performance bottleneck.
Assuming a UNIQUE constraint behaves identically to a PRIMARY KEY, forgetting it allows one NULL and a table can have several.
Skipping normalization entirely for a new transactional schema and paying for it later with data anomalies and inconsistent updates.

followUps.question: What's the difference between 2NF and 3NF in plain terms?
followUps.answer: 2NF only becomes relevant with a composite (multi-column) primary key: every non-key column must depend on the ENTIRE key, not just part of it. 3NF applies more broadly: every non-key column must depend directly on the key, not indirectly through some other non-key column (a transitive dependency) — e.g., if City determines State, State shouldn't live in a table keyed by CustomerId alongside City; it belongs in its own City-keyed table.

followUps.question: When would you deliberately denormalize?
followUps.answer: In read-heavy reporting or analytics scenarios where measured, profiled evidence shows that repeated expensive joins are a genuine bottleneck — you deliberately duplicate data (or maintain a summary/reporting table) to avoid those joins, accepting the added complexity of keeping duplicated data in sync.

followUps.question: What's the risk of ON DELETE CASCADE in a deep referential chain?
followUps.answer: Deleting one parent row can silently cascade through several levels of dependent child tables, potentially deleting far more data than intended — it's worth explicitly mapping out the cascade chain before relying on it in a production schema, especially for anything business-critical.

memoryHack.oneLiner: 1NF = one fact per box; 2NF = depend on the WHOLE key; 3NF = depend on NOTHING but the key. FK = must reference a real registered parent.
memoryHack.memoryPalace: A city permit office: Form Rule 1 says one answer per box, no lists crammed in (1NF); Form Rule 2 says every fact must relate to the FULL building+unit combo, not just the building (2NF); Form Rule 3 says no fact should be smuggled in indirectly through another fact already on the form (3NF) — and the front desk rejects any paperwork naming a landlord not in the city registry (FOREIGN KEY).

bestPractices: Design new transactional schemas to at least 3NF by default, to avoid update anomalies and redundant data.
Use FOREIGN KEY constraints to enforce referential integrity rather than relying on application-level checks alone.
Use ON DELETE CASCADE deliberately and sparingly, mapping out the full cascade chain before relying on it in production.
Denormalize only after profiling shows joins are a genuine, measured bottleneck — and document why the redundancy exists.
Use UNIQUE constraints (not just application checks) for business uniqueness rules like email addresses or SKUs.
performanceTips: Foreign keys benefit from a supporting index on the child table's FK column for efficient JOINs and cascade operations.
Over-normalized schemas can require many joins for common queries — denormalizing specific hot-path reporting tables is a legitimate, measured trade-off.
ON DELETE CASCADE across many tables can turn a single-row delete into a large, slow cascading operation — monitor and index accordingly.

quiz.question: Which normal form specifically addresses partial dependency on a composite key?
quiz.explanation: 2NF requires every non-key column to depend on the entire composite primary key, not just part of it — this is only relevant when the key has multiple columns.

quiz.question: What does 3NF eliminate that 2NF does not?
quiz.explanation: 3NF builds on 2NF by requiring non-key columns to depend only directly on the key, eliminating dependencies that flow indirectly through other non-key columns.

quiz.question: What is a valid reason to denormalize a schema?
options: It's always a best practice from the start
Measured evidence shows expensive joins are a genuine bottleneck in a read-heavy reporting path
To avoid writing FOREIGN KEY constraints
It makes the schema easier to understand in all cases
quiz.explanation: Denormalization is a deliberate, measured trade-off for read performance in specific bottlenecked scenarios, not a default starting design choice.
